newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST--US growth seen moderating through Q1 '99.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST--US growth seen moderating through Q1 '99.

text.p: The rapid pulse of the U.S. economy will gradually weaken to a more moderate rate over the next two years, economists said in the latest Reuters quarterly U.S. economic survey.

The experts projected gross domestic product growth will decelerate gradually to 2.1 percent by first-quarter 1999 from an average forecast of about 3.9 percent in the first quarter of 1997 -- give or take a tenth of a point after the revised international trade data are released on April 25.
Economists said growth over the next eight quarters is expected to moderate across the board, with the greatest drag coming from consumption.

"There will be a slowing of consumption, but it won't show through too much in the first quarter (1997) because of some inventory building," said Peter Kretzmer, senior economist at NationsBanc Capital Markets Inc.
Kretzmer said production will slow by the largest degree in the third quarter and return to trend.
"One of the hallmarks of this expansion has been the rapid adjustment of manufacturing and you will see a slowdown almost immediately," he said.

Kurt Karl, chief economist at WEFA Inc's U.S. forecasting center, agreed. "Business investment is going to come in strong in the first quarter, particularly in the durable equipment, but that will slow down," he said.

So far, however, the U.S. economy showed no signs of substantial easing as it entered its seventh year of economic expansion. Consumers continued to purchase big-ticket items amid a low-interest rate environment.
The Commerce Department said final GDP grew at an annualized rate of 3.8 percent in fourth-quarter 1996, up from a 2.1-percent rate in the previous quarter.
Meanwhile, consumer spending, which makes up about two-thirds of GDP, rose 3.4 percent on an annualized rate in the fourth quarter of 1996. Third-quarter consumer spending rose 0.5 percent.
First-quarter 1997 GDP is slated for release on Wednesday.

In addition, Sohn said that whether or not Congress and the White House succeed in balancing the federal budget by the year 2002, the economy will decelerate as a result.

If an accord to balance the budget is reached, some government spending will likely be sacrificed, Sohn said. If talks to balance the budget break down, then economic growth will also slow because the financial markets will be disappointed, he said.
"So either way, it will cause a slowdown in growth," he said.
"The low interest rate environment and tremendous gains in the employment situation is fueling income and consumer confidence," said Joseph Dziwura, vice president and economist at Sakura Bank, Ltd.
"It's primarily things like income, consumer confidence and sentiment that has really been driving things," he said.
But increases in both interest rates and personal debt are sure to induce consumers to tighten their purse strings, experts said.

In an attempt to stifle future inflation, the Federal Reserve in March boosted short-term interest rates by 25 basis points, its first rate hike in over two years. Many pundits expect the Fed to tighten credit again this year.
"The (economic) drag will most likely come from interest-rate sensitive sectors of the economy," said Sung Won Sohn, chief economist at Norwest Corp.
Sohn said the Fed will lift short-term interest rates at least one more time, probably at the next monetary policy meeting on May 20.
